MetaCheck Report

Inter-trial intervals bias reinforcement learning in humans

2026-11-08 · Metacheck 0.4.3.9

3to fix4to improve0to decide by hand3fine4not applicable

To fix (3)

To fix Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests

What we found

We found 33 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

Show details

We recommend checking the sentences below, and add any missing effect sizes.
In Study 1, participants switched away from the option they had just chosen on 45.1% of trials after a 4 s ITI versus 38.9% after a 1 s ITI (t(95) = 5.54, p < 10⁻⁶).
Specifically, after a win, switching rose from 20.5% to 28.2% (t(95) = 5.89, p < 10⁻⁷), whereas after a loss it was unchanged (69.3% to 70.3%, t(95) = 0.61, p = 0.54; the two effects differed, t(95) = 3.54, p = 0.0006; Fig. 1d).
Specifically, after a win, switching rose from 20.5% to 28.2% (t(95) = 5.89, p < 10⁻⁷), whereas after a loss it was unchanged (69.3% to 70.3%, t(95) = 0.61, p = 0.54; the two effects differed, t(95) = 3.54, p = 0.0006; Fig. 1d).
Specifically, after a win, switching rose from 20.5% to 28.2% (t(95) = 5.89, p < 10⁻⁷), whereas after a loss it was unchanged (69.3% to 70.3%, t(95) = 0.61, p = 0.54; the two effects differed, t(95) = 3.54, p = 0.0006; Fig. 1d).
To see whether the effect was robust to timebound influences, such as the shift from early to late learning and fatigue, we also tested it early and late in the task, in the first and second half of the trials (trials 2-50 and 51-100; Fig. 1e): after a win, switching rose from 26.8% to 32.5% in the first half (t(95) = 3.16, p = 0.002) and from 17.8% to 23.5% in the second (t(95) = 4.05, p < 10⁻³), whereas after a loss it did not change in either half (73.9% to 72.6%, t(95) = 0.67, p = 0.51; 65.2% to 66.4%, t(95) = 0.51, p = 0.61).

Despite this bias, participants learned overall, choosing the option with the highest current reward probability on 47% of trials, against 33% expected by chance (t(95) = 15.7, p < 10⁻²⁷; Fig. 1c).
To ensure the perceptual task did induce cognitive load which reduces replay effects, we demonstrated that participants accurately discriminated the direction of motion during the within-ITI task on 77% of 4 s displays and 58% of 1 s displays (chance 50%; 4 s versus 1 s, paired t(95) = 12.1, p < 10⁻²⁰).
Confirming what we found in Study 1, again we saw that long ITI increased switching behavior (49.9% to 55.9%, t(95) = 5.51, p < 10⁻⁶).

A switch was scored on every trial t > 1 on which a valid choice was registered on both t and t 1 and the option chosen differed from the option chosen on t 1.
The ITI that followed trial t is coded w t = 0 after a 1 s ITI and 1 after a 4 s ITI, so only the long wait enters the models.

To fix Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 74 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 1 of 308 data columns (0%) is documented in a codebook; 307 are not.
  • A codebook was found and parsed (74 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents subject_id, trial, choice while the data has subject_id, prolific_id, model. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.
Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 10 codebook/README/label sources and 308 data columns across 26 files.

A codebook was found and parsed (74 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents subject_id, trial, choice while the data has subject_id, prolific_id, model. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

To fix Reproducibility Check

What we found

  • We assessed AND ran 42 Python code files for reproducibility.
  • 35 Python files skipped as byte-identical duplicates of another file already in the run.
  • 4 of 29 Python scripts ran without error when executed (11 more files are imported by other files, not run on their own).
  • 14 installable Python dependencies detected.
  • 20 statistics stored from the extracted output; 6 of 51 reported tests matched (11.8%).

Note

See the section Reproducibility Check below for the details.

To check (4)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 13 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = 0.54 Specifically, after a win, switching rose from 20.5% to 28.2% (t(95) = 5.89, p < 10⁻⁷), whereas after a loss it was unchanged (69.3% to 70.3%, t(95) = 0.61, p = 0.54; the two effects differed, t(95) = 3.54, p = 0.0006; Fig. 1d).
p = 0.51 To see whether the effect was robust to timebound influences, such as the shift from early to late learning and fatigue, we also tested it early and late in the task, in the first and second half of the trials (trials 2-50 and 51-100; Fig. 1e): after a win, switching rose from 26.8% to 32.5% in the first half (t(95) = 3.16, p = 0.002) and from 17.8% to 23.5% in the second (t(95) = 4.05, p < 10⁻³), whereas after a loss it did not change in either half (73.9% to 72.6%, t(95) = 0.67, p = 0.51; 65.2% to 66.4%, t(95) = 0.51, p = 0.61).
p = 0.61 To see whether the effect was robust to timebound influences, such as the shift from early to late learning and fatigue, we also tested it early and late in the task, in the first and second half of the trials (trials 2-50 and 51-100; Fig. 1e): after a win, switching rose from 26.8% to 32.5% in the first half (t(95) = 3.16, p = 0.002) and from 17.8% to 23.5% in the second (t(95) = 4.05, p < 10⁻³), whereas after a loss it did not change in either half (73.9% to 72.6%, t(95) = 0.67, p = 0.51; 65.2% to 66.4%, t(95) = 0.51, p = 0.61).
p = 0.13 Critically, like in Study 1, the effect was concentrated after a win (33.5% to 39.3%, t(95) = 4.11, p < 10⁻⁴) and did not change reliably after losses (75.9% to 78.1%, t(95) = 1.54, p = 0.13; Fig. 2b).
p = 0.26 Tested early and late in the task, as in Study 1, the effect was again present in both halves (Fig. 2c): after a win, switching rose in both the first half (33.5% to 39.2%, t(95) = 3.18, p = 0.002) and the second (33.6% to 40.0%, t(95) = 3.86, p < 10⁻³), and after a loss in neither (77.6% to 79.9%, t(95) = 1.14, p = 0.26; 74.7% to 73.4%, t(95) = 0.58, p = 0.57).
p = 0.57 Tested early and late in the task, as in Study 1, the effect was again present in both halves (Fig. 2c): after a win, switching rose in both the first half (33.5% to 39.2%, t(95) = 3.18, p = 0.002) and the second (33.6% to 40.0%, t(95) = 3.86, p < 10⁻³), and after a loss in neither (77.6% to 79.9%, t(95) = 1.14, p = 0.26; 74.7% to 73.4%, t(95) = 0.58, p = 0.57).
p = 0.083 Moreover, as in the two previous studies, the effect was significant after wins (29.3% to 36.5%, t(438) = 12.30, p < 10⁻²⁹) and not significant after losses (71.8% to 72.9%, t(438) = 1.74, p = 0.083; Fig. 3a).
p = 0.97 The post-win effect was present there as -well: after a win, switching rose from 27.4% to 32.3% after a long ITI (t(438) = 7.10, p < 10⁻¹¹), close to its size in the first half (33.4% to 40.3%, t(438) = 8.37, p < 10⁻¹⁵), whereas after a loss there was no effect in either half (75.4% to 75.4%, t(438) = 0.03, p = 0.97; 69.4% to 67.8%, t(438) = 1.80, p = 0.07; Fig. 3b).
p = 0.07 The post-win effect was present there as -well: after a win, switching rose from 27.4% to 32.3% after a long ITI (t(438) = 7.10, p < 10⁻¹¹), close to its size in the first half (33.4% to 40.3%, t(438) = 8.37, p < 10⁻¹⁵), whereas after a loss there was no effect in either half (75.4% to 75.4%, t(438) = 0.03, p = 0.97; 69.4% to 67.8%, t(438) = 1.80, p = 0.07; Fig. 3b).
p = 0.16 Neither preregistered test was supported (impulsivity r(437) = 0.05, one-sided p = 0.16; anhedonia r(437) = 0.02 in the wrong direction, one-sided p = 0.62).
p = 0.62 Neither preregistered test was supported (impulsivity r(437) = 0.05, one-sided p = 0.16; anhedonia r(437) = 0.02 in the wrong direction, one-sided p = 0.62).
p = 0.11 An exploratory analysis restricted to post-win trials, where the effect is concentrated, found a small positive association with impulsivity (r(437) = 0.11, p = 0.023; Spearman ρ(437) = 0.13, p = 0.008), which does not survive controlling for the decline in switching over trials (each participant’s ITI slope from the mixed-effects model with the linear trial term: r(437) = 0.08, p = 0.11).
p = 0.23 The post-win trend reported held for every λ between 0.5 and 0.9 in both studies (all p 0.003); the weak post-loss trend in Study 3 did not (p = 0.23 at ≤ λ = 0.5).

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including ‘README’ in the name of your overview document.

Archive Files

The following files are not ZIP archives: parameter_recovery_fit_m12_iti_compete_group_posterior_draws.csv.gz. We recommend the .zip format for archives: only ZIP stores its file listing in a way that lets a tool inspect the contents without downloading the whole archive, so a .zip is more discoverable and re-usable than a .7z, .rar, .tar or .tar.gz.

Registration Points to a Closed Project

1 OSF project (https://osf.io/mr5ek) is referenced by a registration in this manuscript, but it is closed or inaccessible, and no copy of its files could be found anywhere else. Some OSF registrations only describe what was shared, while the actual files live in the project they were registered from — if that project is closed and the registration holds no copy, metacheck cannot list or download its files, and other researchers cannot access them either. Consider making the source project openly available, or re-uploading its files directly into the registration.

Registration’s Source Project Is Closed

1 OSF source project is closed. The files metacheck lists below were not read from it — they were retrieved from the OSF registration’s own copy, which is separate from and unaffected by the project’s access setting. Nothing is currently lost, but this is still worth fixing: a closed source project means the files only survive for as long as the registration’s copy does, and anyone who follows the project link itself (rather than the registration) will find it inaccessible.

  • https://osf.io/ukh58 is closed; its files were retrieved from the OSF registration https://osf.io/6tmja/overview, https://osf.io/6tmja.

Consider making the source project openly available.

Unclassified Files

We could not classify 3 files by name or extension: firestore.rules, firestore.rules, firestore.rules. Add a recognisable keyword (data, code, materials, documentation, output) to the file name, or use a common extension, so both humans and machines can tell what kind of file it is.

Study/Repository Mismatch

The studies named in the manuscript do not match how the repository’s files are grouped: the repository separates out a study (pilot00) not named in the manuscript. Check that every study has its own clearly-named folder or file prefix, and that the folder names match how the manuscript refers to each study.

File Naming

File names should be machine-parseable: no spaces or special characters, and every file should be classifiable by name or extension. We found 4 naming problems that should be fixed, and 4 files with a naming suggestion (not required, but a good habit).

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 20 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 308 columns across 26 data files.

Issues Identified

10 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 26 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script needs a file that another script should have made.

  • make_generalization_figure.py needs fig6a_tomov.png, which plot_fig6a_tomov.py makes.
  • tomov_iti_glmm.py needs tidy.csv, which prepare_tomov2020.py makes.

The other script stopped before it made the file, so fix that script first; this one may then run as well. To make the order clear to readers, number your scripts in the order they run (01_clean.R, 02_model.R), or add one main script that runs the others in order.

Files are missing from your deposit.

  • make_supp_fig2_lag_profile.py reads glmm_twoback_different_fixef.csv.
  • make_study4_figure.py reads switching_by_outcome.json.
  • make_supp_table1.py reads model_comparison_loo.csv.

  • analyze_agents.py reads trials.csv.
  • make_manuscript_figures.py reads learning_stats.json.
  • plot_fig6a_tomov.py reads model_table.csv.

The script stops at the line that reads the file.

  1. Find the file on your computer.
  2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it.
  3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it.

Your code was written for older versions of its packages.

  • 19_exploration_marker_ppc.py: “AttributeError: module ‘matplotlib.style’ has no attribute ‘core’”

A function or option has changed since you wrote the code, so it stops with today’s version of the package.

  1. In R, run renv::init() in your project and add the renv.lock file this creates to the deposit; in Python, run pip freeze > requirements.txt and add that file.
  2. State your version of R or Python in the README.
  3. Better still, update the code so it also works with current versions.

A script downloads data while it runs.

  • pull_ai_data.py
  • run_agents.py

Online files can move, change or disappear. Save the downloaded files, add them to the deposit, and let the script read the saved copies.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The “Plausible” column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output’s own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

Thus, we used the same design as in Study 1, except here, participants completed a perceptual decisionmaking task where they needed to report whether the dominant motion of moving dots was upward or downward during the ITI to reduce any effect of replay (Fig. 2a).

In order to confirm that we used valid trials to estimate switching rates, we sought to remove trials where participants were likely still answering the perceptual task when the next choice screen appeared.

To validate these choices were in fact left-over choices from the perceptual task during the ITI, and should be discarded, we show how these choices tended to ignore the values participants had learned, unlike slower choices (Fig. 2d-f).

Choices also depended on what participants had chosen before, reflecting choice perseveration.

For each generating model, five synthetic data sets of 50 participants were simulated, each participant playing a randomly chosen real participant’s task with parameters spread evenly over the full range of every parameter (Latin-hypercube sampling over the ranges of d).

We thus predicted that the ITI effect would be larger when participants were exploring options they had not recently visited and were more uncertain of.

Participants in all four studies were recruited through Prolific 31 .

They also had to report English as a fluent language and have a Prolific approval rate of 95-100%.

Each study excluded from its recruitment pool everyone who had taken part in an earlier study or pilot of the project, so no participant took part in more than one study.

All studies were approved by the Human Subjects Institutional Review Board (HSIRB) of Bar-Ilan University (approval no. 310725687), and all participants gave informed consent online before starting the task.

In Study 1, the 96 analyzed participants were aged 24 to 81 years (M = 46.2, SD = 13.0); 54 were women and 42 men.

For Studies 2 and 3, the figures below describe everyone who submitted the study on Prolific (99 and 481 people), not only the analyzed samples.

There were 246 men and 231 women, and four participants preferred not to report their sex.

Such choices were impossibly fast, did not follow the values the participant had learned and switched at the chance level of 2/3 (Fig. 2d-f).

Trials on which no response was registered within the deadline were recorded as misses, and participants were told in advance that the task would end if they accumulated five misses.

All participants were exposed to the same predetermined trajectories, so the reward probabilities changed identically, and at the same points in the task, for everyone.

Before the main task, participants completed six practice trials with a different set of images and a different set of reward trajectories, and they were told that the images would change.

Every parameter of that synthetic participant was drawn independently and uniformly over its full range, and the synthetic participants were refitted with the same hierarchy.

For model recovery among the three ITI models, five datasets of 50 synthetic participants were simulated from each model.

Thirty-one participants completed two scanned sessions of a two-armed bandit in which each ten-trial run presented a new pair of arms with fixed but unknown means, under four risk conditions.

Ethics approval statement:

All studies were approved by the Human Subjects Institutional Review Board (HSIRB) of Bar-Ilan University (approval no. 310725687), and all participants gave informed consent online before starting the task.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

description Background
Classic reinforcement learning models, such as the Rescorla - Wagner model, focus primarily on reward: whether outcomes are better or worse than expected, and how value estimates should be updated accordingly. However, when participants engage in decision-making tasks, a key component of real-world choice is often overlooked - time. Time spent on a given action is time not spent on alternatives, making it a meaningful opportunity cost that may shape behavior.
While prior work has shown that fatigue and prolonged task engagement can alter decision-making processes over time, it remains largely unclear whether the fine-grained temporal structure of a task - specifically inter-trial intervals (ITIs) - systematically influences learning and choice. Similar to how individuals learn expected value from reward feedback, they may also learn expectations about time based on ITI feedback, and integrate these estimates to maximize reward rate per unit time.
In a prior study from our lab, we directly tested this idea using a three-armed restless bandit task in which ITI duration (1s vs. 4s) was manipulated within-subject. Across two experiments (N = 100 each), we found that longer ITIs increased the likelihood of switching away from the previously selected option, suggesting that participants assign a cost to actions that precede longer delays. To account for this effect, we developed a series of computational models and showed that participants maintain separate expectations over reward and time, integrating them at the moment of decision. In particular, an ITI Learn model—incorporating dynamically updated time expectations and time prediction errors—provided the best fit to behavior, outperforming competing models. In that study, the effect was observed in both task variants (with and without a perceptual distractor during the ITI), though it was somewhat stronger in the no-distractor version. Accordingly, the present study adopts the no-distractor version to maximize sensitivity to the effect. Given its superior fit and its ability to capture ITI-dependent modulation of choice, the ITI Learn model is expected to provide a strong account of behavior in the current data as well.
Building on these findings, the current study tests whether ITIs influence decision policies in a general adult sample, and whether individual differences in transdiagnostic traits modulate this effect. We focus on impulsivity and anhedonia, as they make distinct - and partially opposing - predictions regarding sensitivity to time costs. First, we aim to replicate the core finding that longer ITIs increase switching behavior. Second, we predict that impulsivity will be positively associated with the magnitude of this ITI effect, reflecting heightened sensitivity to delays. Third, we predict that anhedonia will be negatively associated with the ITI effect, reflecting reduced sensitivity to temporal differences. As an exploratory analysis, we may also examine an interaction between impulsivity and anhedonia, although primary analyses will focus on these associations separately.
Participants
A total of 472 adult participants will be recruited via Prolific. All participants will provide informed consent and self-confirm no history of neurological or psychiatric diagnoses. Sample size was determined based on planned power analyses for the primary correlational hypotheses.
Replicating main effect: Longer ITI promotes switching away from last action.
Power was estimated by parametric Monte-Carlo simulation. Reference fixed- and random-effects parameters were obtained by fitting the planned generalised linear mixed model
is_shift ~ 1 + prev_ITI + (1 + prev_ITI | subject), family = binomial(logit),
to combined pilot data from two studies (N = 180 subjects, 17,627 trials, after excluding subjects performing at or below chance). The fitted ITI fixed-effect was b = 0.074 in log-odds per second of inter-trial interval (Wald SE = 0.012, LRT χ²(1) = 33.5, p = 7.1 × 10⁻⁹; parametric-bootstrap LRT p < 0.001, 1000 simulations; profile-likelihood 95% CI [0.050, 0.098]). The estimated random-effects covariance was used as-is (intercept SD = 0.91, slope SD = 0.073, r = −0.30).
For each of 100 simulated samples of N = 472 subjects, trial counts per subject and the proportion of long-ITI trials per subject were drawn (with replacement) from the empirical distribution; subject-specific intercepts and slopes were drawn from the estimated random-effects MVN; trial-level shift responses were generated under the fitted logistic GLMM. Each simulated dataset was fit with the full model and with a nested null model omitting the prev_ITI fixed effect, and inference was carried out using a likelihood-ratio test (preferred over Wald because Wald is anti-conservative in GLMMs). Power was defined as the proportion of simulations with LRT p < .05.
At N = 472, estimated power for the ITI effect was >0.99 (100/100 simulations significant; median simulated p = 6.3 × 10⁻²¹).
Individual differences
Specifically, using a one-tailed correlation test with α = .05, power = .95, and an assumed effect size of r = .15, G*Power estimated a required sample size of 472 participants.
Task Design
Participants will complete a 100-trial, three-armed restless bandit task in which the reward probabilities of each arm drift gradually according to a fixed random-walk process. The key manipulation is ITI length, varied within-subjects across short and long intervals. After each choice and reward feedback, the next trial begins after the assigned interval. We use the no-distractor version of the task, in which no perceptual filler appears during the ITI, since prior results showed a slightly stronger effect under this condition, although the effect was present in both variants.
Measures
Behavioral measures will include choice patterns across trials, switching rates (stay versus shift behavior), and reaction times. Participants will also complete self-report questionnaires assessing impulsivity and anhedonia, which we treat as transdiagnostic traits rather than categorical diagnoses.
Modeling Approach
We will compare a baseline Rescorla–Wagner model against ITI-augmented alternatives. The primary model is the ITI Learn model described above, which won the model comparison in our prior anxiety study and which we therefore expect to provide the best account here as well. To assess robustness, we will run a sensitivity analysis and apply an updated modeling procedure that allows different best-fitting models per participant rather than enforcing a single model across the sample. 		NA
research_questions NA WE have the same core hypothesis - that longer ITI promotes switching in a 3-armed bandit task - and here like our 3 previous studies (https://osf.io/6tmja/ most recent and highlights prior two studies), we use the same task and reward trajectory. We simply alter the ITI sequence. We will use the same mixed model as before, except now control for trial number influencing switching rate (since we later observed switching declines over the task). WE will do so both using frequentists and bayesian methods for sensitivity analysis to show findings our robust to this methods choice.

We seek to replicate our primary hypothesis in a study n=132. This is slightly greater than the our original studies with n=100, to deal with potential drop-out rates.

data_collection_procedures NA Collecting on Prolific from English-speaking countries. Made sure participants did not participate in any earlier version of this project.
sample_size NA 132
sample_size_rationale NA Over-powered for previous main effect (n=100) due to ITI-sequence change which might slightly mitigate the effect.
stopping_rule NA None
manipulated_variables NA ITI is the main manipulated variable - ensure some ITIs are 1s and some are 4s (each 50% representation in our 100-trial task, now slightly more 1s early on).
measured_variables NA Sensitivity of choice-switching to ITI length, controlling for trial number.
indices NA Mixed-effects models. Every mixed-effects regression was fitted as a Bayesian model in PyMC by the No-U-Turn sampler (nutpie; 4 chains × 1,000 draws after 1,000 warm-up iterations, target acceptance 0.9; github_repo/analysis_common/bayes_glmm.py). The preregistered model was extended by a linear effect of trial number, which absorbs the decline in switching over the session:
logit P(switch_ij) = (β0 + u0,j) + (βITI + uITI,j) · ITI_ij + (βT + uT,j) · trial_ij
where ITI_ij is the prior ITI of participant j’s choice i in seconds and trial_ij is the trial number centred and scaled per 50 trials ((t − 50.5)/50), each entering as a fixed effect and a participant-level random slope. Other contrasts (for example a long interval after the choice two trials back) enter in the same way, with the trial term in every model. Priors were N(0, 1.5) on the intercept, N(0, 1) on the other fixed effects and half-normal(1) on the random-effect standard deviations. The random effects were independent: the random interval slope varies little between participants, so its correlations with the other random effects were not identified and did not mix. We report the posterior mean, the 95% credible interval (CrI), the odds ratio for 4 s against 1 s, and the two-sided posterior tail probability, 2 × min(P(β > 0), P(β < 0)), in place of a p value. Every model reported has R̂ ≤ 1.1 for its fixed effects and random-effect standard deviations. Effects after wins and after losses were estimated in those trials separately, and their difference by the prior ITI × previous outcome interaction in all trials.
statistical_tests NA Mixed-effects models. How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

We try to exclude figure and table notes like “* p < .05”, but may not succeed at excluding all false positives.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Although we know humans attempt to maximize reward per unit time when foraging, it remains unclear how the common practice of varying waiting time via inter-trial intervals (ITI) impacts reinforcement learning. Here, we tested several hypotheses concerning how time to wait during the ITI impacts reinforcement learning, including replay of recent outcomes, sensory decay of action representations, and discounting of action values due to added time costs. To test which of these accounts explains how ITIs impact reinforcement learning, we conducted a series of bandit-style tasks in which the ITI was either 1 or 4 seconds, expecting longer ITIs to allow replay that strengthens recent learning. Instead, across four studies (n = 96, 96, 439 and 117), a longer ITI made people more likely to change their last choice selectively after wins but not after losses. To explain why this effect occurs, we used computational modeling to demonstrate how the ITI cost competes with learned value for control of the next choice, with time costs impacting choice more when learned values were more uncertain. The effect of ITIs on choice generalized to a public fMRI dataset with jittered ITIs, and was absent in language-model agents playing our task. Taken together, our results suggest that ITIs bias human reinforcement learning, where people try to reduce uncontrollable time costs through switching to a new choice.

Introduction

Humans dislike waiting. Imagine that when eating pizza, you were forced to wait for longer intervals between each bite than what you would naturally choose. Such waiting without receiving expected reward (a tasty bite) would likely be disappointing. This thought experiment is unusual because it contrasts with the typical scenario where, when acting in the world, we control how much reward we experience over time. Computational work on foraging has formalized how waiting time impacts decision-making 1, 2 , wherein humans balance exploiting their current environment for reward versus exploring a new environment's potential reward by maximizing their reward per unit time 3, 4 . The Marginal-Value Theorem provides this objective that defines optimal foraging, and explains why waiting longer without reward in one's current environment increases the opportunity cost of foregoing switching to a new environment.

Despite this seminal work on how time and reward jointly impact decision-making, the impact of waiting time on choices has been largely neglected in human reinforcement learning (RL) 5 . In simple bandit-style tasks, humans make many decisions, receive rewards or punishments after those decisions, and must wait between decisions 6 . Such waiting time, typically referred to as the inter-trial interval (ITI), is widely neglected as a meaningful task parameter that might alter learning and decision-making dynamics. Indeed, as most ITIs are only on the scale of seconds, one might suspect that such small differences are overlooked by participants. For this reason, researchers typically vary the ITI to measure neural signals that covary with latent learning variables, such as the prediction error (deviation between expected and actual outcome), without any explicit modeling or consideration as to how the range of ITIs might impact learning and decisionmaking 7, 8.

Recent work, however, does indeed suggest that waiting time impacts the learning algorithm used to make decisions. For example, it has been shown that mice that choose their own ITIs have a different learning strategy after a chosen longer waiting time versus a shorter one 9 . Whereas short ITIs are followed by decisions that arise from a simple win-stay, lose-shift decision strategy, longer wait times are followed by an integrative learning rule, where mice average their expected reward for a given action over its outcome history. In other words, longer chosen waiting time in mice reflects a normative shift toward a lower learning rate that generates expected values in line with the true reward rate. Critically, because ITIs were chosen and not experimentally manipulated, such a finding may reflect the influence of decision strategy on the ITI rather than a causal effect of the ITI on reinforcement learning.

In humans, only longer intervals beyond the ITI, from rest periods between task phases [10] [11] [12] [13] to overnight sleep 14 , have been explored to determine how the replaying of prior experience might impact offline learning and subsequent decisions. In that work, it is clear that long periods between decisions confer consolidation of prior knowledge, whereby individuals can leverage replay of prior experience to infer the latent rules and structure required to make optimal choices 12, 13.

The impact of shorter ITIs on decision making has only been explored in tasks involving perceptual decision-making in the absence of learning. For example, it has been shown that longer wait times dissipate recent perceptual representations, described by a representational decay model 15, 16 . This has been applied to action representations, where individuals are more likely to switch to a new action after a single longer ITI 17, 18.

Despite this important work, it remains unclear whether in human RL tasks, one would see evidence of replay of recent outcomes, of action-representation decay, or of time costs entering the valuation of actions, as a function of longer ITIs. Unlike existing replay work, the ITIs in typical RL experiments are much shorter, and they are interrupted by ongoing task experience. On the other hand, unlike perceptual decision making work, typical RL tasks involve non-independent trials that require participants to learn the latent reward structure. And, ultimately, the only work to assess how time-costs impact the value of decisions comes from foraging paradigms, which do not involve the multi-action choice problem endemic to reinforcement learning.

To address these gaps in order to determine the impact of waiting time on learning and decision making, we sought to assess how experimentally varying the ITI (1 or 4 seconds) impacts how humans learn in bandit-style tasks used in human RL. Although originally hypothesizing that we would see evidence of greater replay under longer ITIs, we instead discovered that humans are biased to switch to new choices after longer ITIs, particularly after a reward. We then replicated these findings in three independent datasets using the same task, showed that our core finding generalized to an existing fMRI dataset, and demonstrated that AI models do not exhibit the same key effect of ITI on choice.

To explain the mechanism giving rise to this behavior, we developed a computational model that explains how humans act like foragers in RL tasks, treating the time spent waiting after an action as a cost of that action. The time cost during a long wait competes with the learned value of each option for control of the next choice, selectively weakening the reinforcement of a rewarded action, explaining whylonger waits increased switching after wins and not after losses. The shift was also strongest when the last choice was exploratory, that is, when learned values were most uncertain.

We regard such switching behavior as a bias because the ITIs in the task were random with respect to choices, and thus choosing to switch to a new action did not on average result in shorter waiting time. Below, we describe the series of studies that evidences this model where time and value compete for behavioral control during RL. In doing so, we rule out compelling alternative replay, sensory decay and value-time integrated learning accounts of the impact of ITIs on reinforcement learning.

Results

We tested how ITIs might impact learning and decision-making in a three-armed bandit task (Fig. 1) in four separate studies (Study 1, n = 96; Study 2, n = 96; Study 3, preregistered, n = 439; Study 4, preregistered, n = 117). Our initial hypothesis concerned the potential role replay might play during ITIs. Specifically, we expected that, if given more time to think during the ITI, offline learning over one's remembered action-outcome sequences might augment the rate of learning for recent outcomes. For example, if experiencing a positive outcome, longer ITI would increase the tendency to stay with one's prior action due to recencyweighted sampling of memory. Indeed, prior research suggests that offline learning over remembered outcomes facilitates learning, and is biased by recent outcomes 10, 19.

In contrast to our initial hypothesis, results showed that longer ITI increased switching behavior. In Study 1, participants switched away from the option they had just chosen on 45.1% of trials after a 4 s ITI versus 38.9% after a 1 s ITI (t(95) = 5.54, p < 10⁻⁶). In fact, the effect was larger after a win, suggesting that replaying the last outcome to induce offline learning was not evident. Specifically, after a win, switching rose from 20.5% to 28.2% (t(95) = 5.89, p < 10⁻⁷), whereas after a loss it was unchanged (69.3% to 70.3%, t(95) = 0.61, p = 0.54; the two effects differed, t(95) = 3.54, p = 0.0006; Fig. 1d). To see whether the effect was robust to timebound influences, such as the shift from early to late learning and fatigue, we also tested it early and late in the task, in the first and second half of the trials (trials 2-50 and 51-100; Fig. 1e): after a win, switching rose from 26.8% to 32.5% in the first half (t(95) = 3.16, p = 0.002) and from 17.8% to 23.5% in the second (t(95) = 4.05, p < 10⁻³), whereas after a loss it did not change in either half (73.9% to 72.6%, t(95) = 0.67, p = 0.51; 65.2% to 66.4%, t(95) = 0.51, p = 0.61). Despite this bias, participants learned overall, choosing the option with the highest current reward probability on 47% of trials, against 33% expected by chance (t(95) = 15.7, p < 10⁻²⁷; Fig. 1c).
