To rule out whether the observed relation between ITI and switching behavior was mediated by replay, we conducted a second study wherein individuals engaged in a secondary task during the ITI. As in prior work on offline replay, a demanding secondary task reduces replay of past experiences 20 . Thus, we used the same design as in Study 1, except here, participants completed a perceptual decisionmaking task where they needed to report whether the dominant motion of moving dots was upward or downward during the ITI to reduce any effect of replay (Fig. 2a). To ensure the perceptual task did induce cognitive load which reduces replay effects, we demonstrated that participants accurately discriminated the direction of motion during the within-ITI task on 77% of 4 s displays and 58% of 1 s displays (chance 50%; 4 s versus 1 s, paired t(95) = 12.1, p < 10⁻²⁰).

In order to confirm that we used valid trials to estimate switching rates, we sought to remove trials where participants were likely still answering the perceptual task when the next choice screen appeared. A downward trial was answered by pressing Q, T and P together, the three keys used to choose any bandit, and when the display ended before the press, the press landed on the choice screen, where the first of the three keys to go down registered as a choice. After a missed downward display at 1 s, 24% of the next choices came within 250 ms (likely too fast) of the choice screen and 8% within 50 ms. To validate these choices were in fact left-over choices from the perceptual task during the ITI, and should be discarded, we show how these choices tended to ignore the values participants had learned, unlike slower choices (Fig. 2d-f). Such responses were far more common than in Study 1 (after the short ITI 11.3% of choices in Study 2 came within 250 ms, compared to 2.5% in Study 1). We therefore treated every Study 2 choice faster than 250 ms (6.7% of choices) as a missed trial (Methods).

Confirming what we found in Study 1, again we saw that long ITI increased switching behavior (49.9% to 55.9%, t(95) = 5.51, p < 10⁻⁶). Critically, like in Study 1, the effect was concentrated after a win (33.5% to 39.3%, t(95) = 4.11, p < 10⁻⁴) and did not change reliably after losses (75.9% to 78.1%, t(95) = 1.54, p = 0.13; Fig. 2b). Tested early and late in the task, as in Study 1, the effect was again present in both halves (Fig. 2c): after a win, switching rose in both the first half (33.5% to 39.2%, t(95) = 3.18, p = 0.002) and the second (33.6% to 40.0%, t(95) = 3.86, p < 10⁻³), and after a loss in neither (77.6% to 79.9%, t(95) = 1.14, p = 0.26; 74.7% to 73.4%, t(95) = 0.58, p = 0.57). Replicating our original findings, longer ITI appears to increase switching even when a demanding task occurs during the ITI. 1, except that the outcome was followed by a 0.5 s fixation and then by a random-dot-motion display (500 dots, 7% coherence, net motion upward or downward) that lasted for the whole ITI of 1 s or 4 s. Participants pressed Q, T and P together for downward motion and withheld a response for upward motion, without feedback. We next sought to preregister our key hypothesis in a large, online sample in order to both ensure findings generalize and to determine whether any individual differences moderate the effect. We confirmed in these data that, as hypothesized, switching rose after long ITIs (46.0% to 51.9%, t(438) = 12.30, p < 10⁻²⁹). Moreover, as in the two previous studies, the effect was significant after wins (29.3% to 36.5%, t(438) = 12.30, p < 10⁻²⁹) and not significant after losses (71.8% to 72.9%, t(438) = 1.74, p = 0.083; Fig. 3a).

Before asking what mechanism produces the bias, we first had to rule out an artifact specific to our design that we discovered while analyzing the data in Study 3. Switching is not stationary, likely due to participants' uncertainty varying over the task [21] [22] [23] . Indeed, in Study 3, switching fell from 62% in the first twenty trials (likely where participants explore to reduce uncertainty) to 40% in the last twenty, steeply at first and then more slowly (Fig. 3c). This trend in switching happened to coincide with our random sequence-generation of ITIs, where 4-second ITIs happened to be more likely at the start of the task.

We therefore asked whether the ITI effect survives once this decline in switching over trials is modeled. We fitted the preregistered mixed-effects logistic regression of switching on the preceding ITI with trial number added as both a fixed and random (by participant) effect. After controlling for this declining trend, the ITI effect on switching held in Study 3 (b = 0.040, CI = [0.025, 0.055]). Every test of the ITI below uses this mixed-effects model with its linear trial term.

Testing the effect early and late in the task, as in Studies 1 and 2, supports the same conclusion without relying on the trial term. The confound lies in the first half of the session: the first forty trials held 70% and 60% long ITIs, and this is where switching, and presumably exploration, was highest. From trial 41 on, the sequence placed 40% long ITIs in every block of twenty trials and switching had largely leveled off, so that in the second half (trials 51-100) long ITIs and early exploration no longer coincided (correlation between a long ITI and trial number 0.05, against 0.15 in the first half). The post-win effect was present there as -well: after a win, switching rose from 27.4% to 32.3% after a long ITI (t(438) = 7.10, p < 10⁻¹¹), close to its size in the first half (33.4% to 40.3%, t(438) = 8.37, p < 10⁻¹⁵), whereas after a loss there was no effect in either half (75.4% to 75.4%, t(438) = 0.03, p = 0.97; 69.4% to 67.8%, t(438) = 1.80, p = 0.07; Fig. 3b). The effect after wins therefore does not depend on the part of the session in which early exploration and long ITIs were confounded.

To determine the underlying mechanism giving rise to our replicated ITI effect, we formulated three classes of models that each make unique behavioral predictions. The first, inspired by resource-rational and foraging accounts of decision-making, treats time as a cost: the value of an action combines its expected reward, which is to be maximized, and its expected waiting time, the ITI, which is to be reduced. If this were in fact true, then participants should be more willing to abandon actions that have recently been followed by longer ITIs. However, there could be various ways in which the ITI cost impacts choices. If the wait is simply subtracted from the reward it follows, its effect (on the log-odds scale) should be equivalent after a win and a loss. If instead the ITI cost competes with learned value for control over the next choice, its impact aligns with that of a loss but is at-odds with that of a win. An asymmetry between wins and losses is therefore the signature that separates these two ways in which ITI costs and learned values are integrated in the learning process (Methods).

The second account of how time might bias decision-making draws inspiration from perceptual decision-making, where time decays biases to choose the last action taken. This inherently is value-independent, and thus should act not on a value representation, but on choice perseveration. Thus, regardless of whether a win or loss occurred, the bias in switching after a long ITI should be the same.

Finally, a third possibility is that participants learn how long waits are in the task as a whole, and that this global expectation, rather than the wait that followed the last action, drives switching. Unlike the other two, it predicts that an earlier ITI should affect the tendency to take actions other than the action preceding it.

We first sought to rule out the global ITI cost account, which on its face is a less sensible foraging-like strategy than treating each action as its own environment. Specifically, if global time inherently treats all actions as belonging to a single environment, switching cannot reduce time costs (one is still switching within the same environment). We thus tested whether the key prediction of this account was present in the current data, wherein a long ITI after an earlier choice should raise the tendency to leave a different action than the one preceding that prior ITI. By comparing trials on which the option chosen two trials back differed from the option chosen last, we asked whether the ITI that followed that earlier choice predicted current-trial switching. A global account predicts that this earlier ITI should raise switching much as the last one does. Like the main effect, this test inherits the decline in switching over trials, so we used the same mixed-effects model with its linear trial term. The earlier ITI did not predict switching in Study 3 (b = 0.025, CI = [ 0.040, 0.090]), and neither did the ITIs after the choices three and four trials back (Supplementary Fig. 1). Switching depends on the ITI just elapsed and not on earlier ones, so we found no model-agnostic signature of a global expectation.

The ITI-on-choice-bias account, by contrast, makes a prediction about the previous choice irrespective of the reward that came after it. Thus, the effect of a longer ITI should raise switching after a win and after a loss alike (Fig. 3d, middle). In contrast to this prediction in Study 3, the long ITI raised the odds of switching after wins (odds ratio 1.44, CI = [1.33, 1.56]) and not after losses (0.95, CI = [0.88, 1.02]; ITI × outcome interaction b = 0.145, CI = [0.112, 0.178]).

Such an asymmetry is predicted when the ITI competes with value for control of the next choice. To specify exactly how value and time effects are integrated to impact choice behavior, we formalized a series of computational models in which reward and time were either integrated in a combined learning target (additive time cost) or as separate and competing influences on their associated action. a, Switching after a 1 s and after a 4 s ITI, after a win and after a loss (n = 439; mean ± s.e.m. across participants; paired t tests). b, The same contrast in the first and the second half of the session (trials 2-50 and 51-100; mean ± s.e.m. across participants; paired t tests). c, Probability of switching on every trial (mean ± s.e.m. across participants), colored by the ITI that preceded that trial (red, 4 s; blue, 1 s), with a 9-trial moving average (black). The strip below shows the full, fixed sequence of ITIs. The sequence placed 70%, 60%, 40%, 40% and 40% long ITIs in successive blocks of twenty trials.

To test these mechanistic accounts of the ITI impact on learning and choice, we built a series of reinforcement-learning models fitted to choice data in Study 3, the preregistered study with the largest sample. Each component was kept only if it improved out-of-sample predictive accuracy, and each addition to the model was simulated to show it can produce its intended qualitative signature of behavior that real participants displayed (Methods; Fig. 4a,b; Supplementary Table 1). Models were fitted as hierarchical Bayesian models and compared by Paretosmoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out cross-validation, summarized by the expected log predictive density (ELPD).

Our model comparison first established that that participants did indeed learn from outcomes, and thus are sensitive to the value of choices. A Rescorla-Wagner learner predicted choices far better than fixed preferences for the three options (ELPD difference +7,518, SE 121). Separate learning rates for wins and losses improved it further (+346, SE 35), and so did value decay, which lets the values of unchosen options drift back toward a neutral prior (+1,575, SE 66). The learning models also resembled choices better than models with a constant intercept fit to each choice (root-mean-square error 0.035 to 0.042, against 0.068; Fig. 4b).

Choices also depended on what participants had chosen before, reflecting choice perseveration. We compared two ways of capturing this, each added to the value learner: a constant bias toward repeating the option chosen last, and a choice kernel, which keeps a running trace of how often each option has been chosen recently and adds it, weighted, to the decision value of every option 24 . The choice kernel fit choices better (+717.3 over the value-decay model, SE 42.7, against +634.1, SE 33.8, for the constant stay bias; difference +83.2, SE 48.4), yet neither fully reproduced how much more often participants switched after a switch than after a stay (Fig. 4b) which left added variance to explain switching behavior.

Switching was in part strategic. Only 38.6% of the switches returned to the most recently chosen alternative (50% if they had chosen at random between the two alternatives), whereas the choice-kernel model predicted 51.7%. Participants instead tended to switch to the option they had chosen furthest back. A novelty bonus for that option was added, which improved qualitative model predictions (Fig. 4b), and model fit (+913.7, SE 44.4).

Switching also declined over trials, which likely reflected that general task uncertainty fell over the course of learning. To model declining uncertainty, we added a parameter which allowed the inverse temperature to change log-linearly over trials, which improved performance (+559.8, SE 35.7). This fit better than allowing a decreasing trend in the weight of the choice kernel, which improved on the novelty model by only +114.7 (SE 15.7; difference between the two trends +445.1, SE 37.0). Qualitatively, the model with a dynamic inverse temperature also followed the decline in switching more closely (Fig. 4b). Every participant was simulated 20 times from their posterior-mean parameters in their own task environment (reward walks, ITI sequence and missed trials); points and lines, mean over simulations; error bars and bands, 95% range; dashed lines and black points, data. c, The effect of the ITI on switching in Study 3, the ITI slope in log-odds per second from the preregistered mixed model with a linear trend over the session, over all trials, after wins and after losses, in the data and in data simulated from each model. d, Parameter recovery of the best-fitting model, ITI competes with value. One synthetic participant per real participant played that participant's task environment with every parameter drawn independently and uniformly over its full range, and was refitted by NUTS with the priors and settings of the real data. Recovered participant posterior means are plotted against generating values. The dashed line is the identity, the gray band marks the range of the fitted participant estimates, and the Pearson correlation is shown above each panel. e, Model recovery among the three ITI models. For each generating model, five synthetic data sets of 50 participants were simulated, each participant playing a randomly chosen real participant's task with parameters spread evenly over the full range of every parameter (Latin-hypercube sampling over the ranges of d). All three models were fitted to every data set by NUTS, and a data set is won by the model with the highest summed ELPD. Points show the ELPD of the generating model minus that of the better of the other two (± 2 SE of the participant-level difference), one per data set. The number above each model is how many of its data sets it won. f, How the ITI effect is strengthened under greater value uncertainty. The effect of the ITI on switching (the probability after a 4 s ITI minus after a 1 s ITI) by quintile of u = 1/(1 + n) for the option chosen on the trial before the ITI (n, a count of the option's earlier choices that grows by one when it is chosen and loses a fraction 0.85 of its size on every trial it is not; quintiles within participant and outcome, 1 most exploitative, 5 most exploratory), after a win and after a loss, in Studies 3 and 4.

To ultimately determine how ITIs impacted switching behavior, we first asked whether the effect of longer ITIs on choice varied with any task feature prior to fitting a new model. We hypothesized that the ITI effect might be stronger when value learning is a less reliable source of evidence. We thus predicted that the ITI effect would be larger when participants were exploring options they had not recently visited and were more uncertain of. As a model-agnostic proxy for exploratory versus exploitative state we quantified how exploratory the option chosen on the trial before the ITI was as u = 1/(1 + n), where n counts the option's earlier choices (Methods; the proxy is consistent with the explore and exploit states of a hidden Markov model of choices). After wins, the effect of the ITI grew with u (Fig. 4f), from +0.048 in the most exploitative quintile of each participant's trials to +0.083 in the most exploratory quintile (per-participant trend across quintiles, t(438) = 3.41, p = 0.0007). After losses it rose only from 0.036 to 0.001 --(t(438) = 2.01, p = 0.045).

These results suggest that the ITI impacts choice most when value is a less reliable guide for choice. We therefore compared three ways in which the ITI could enter the model (Methods). In the first, the ITI-as-learning-target model (an additive time cost), the long wait that followed an outcome is subtracted from the value learned from it, by the same amount after a win and after a loss. In the second, the ITI-onchoice-bias model, the ITI is insensitive to value and modulates the choice-bias term. The third, the ITI-competes-with-value model, was built on the prior exploration result. When people explore, their choices are by definition less governed by learned value, and random exploration is commonly modeled as a lower weight on value 6, 22 . In this model the weight of a decision is shared between two sources of evidence. One is the learned value of each option, and the other is the ITI just experienced, which counts against the option chosen before it. After a long ITI, part of the weight moves from value to the wait. The share that moves grows with how exploratory that choice was (u = 1/(1 + n), with n here the number of times in a row the option had just been chosen; Methods). Because the total weight is fixed, whatever exploration takes from value goes to time. Importantly, in all models, we used only the last ITI, and not a running estimate of expected ITI, given model-agnostic evidence that only the last ITI predicted current choices (Supplementary Note 1; Supplementary Fig. 2).

We then compared the three ITI models with the model without an ITI term and with each other (Fig. 4a). In Study 3 the ITI-competes-with-value model was the best model overall. It improved on the model without an ITI term by 118.2 (SE 16.8), on the ITI-as-learning-target model by 104.1 (SE 16.9) and on the ITI-onchoice-bias model by 110.9 (SE 16.5). The ITI-as-learning-target model itself improved on the model without an ITI term by 14.1 (SE 8.7), and the ITI-on-choicebias model by 7.3 (SE 5.3).

As a sensitivity analysis to the ELPD comparison, random-effects Bayesian model selection also favored the ITI-competes-with-value model (protected exceedance probability, PXP > 0.99). In this model, a long ITI after a switch to an option moved a share κ = 0.096 (CI = [0.066, 0.126]) of the weight of the next decision from value to the wait. The share halved after two choices of the option in a row and fell further after longer runs. The ITI terms of the other two models were small. A long ITI weakened the choice bias (γ = 0.097, CI = [ 0.169, 0.030]) or lowered the --value learned from the outcome before it (c = 0.060, CI = [0.027, 0.094], on outcomes coded ±1). The winning model, although containing 9 parameters, had good parameter recovery (Fig. 4d), including specifically the ITI weight κ recovered with r = 0.80 (0.59 within the range of the fitted participant estimates) and the other parameters with r from 0.65 (the learning rate after a win) to 0.92 (the novelty bonus). We also show that each ITI model can be recovered well against each other (Fig. 4e).

Simulated from its fitted parameters and analyzed with the same mixed-effects model as the real data, the ITI-competes-with-value model came closest to the ITI effect of Study 3 (Fig. 4c). It thus reproduced the asymmetry between outcomes without a parameter for the outcome. The ITI-competes-with-value model was also the only model whose effect after wins grew with exploratory state (Fig. 4f), with no such trend after losses.

Response times, which the models were not fitted to, showed the same asymmetry as choices, as the ITI-competes-with-value model predicts. In Study 3, after a win a long ITI slowed staying relative to switching (interaction of ITI and stay on log response time, +0.052, CI = [0.035, 0.069]), and after a loss it did not ( 0.019, CI = -[ 0.040, 0.001]; three-way interaction of ITI, stay and outcome +0.073, CI = [0.047, -0.100]; Bayesian linear mixed model with trial number as a fixed effect and participant random slope).

To assess individual differences, we hypothesized and preregistered that trait impulsivity would be positively associated with the effect of time on choice, given that they may have higher opportunity costs to foregoing new opportunities in their environment, and anhedonia would show the opposite effect. Neither preregistered test was supported (impulsivity r(437) = 0.05, one-sided p = 0.16; anhedonia r(437) = 0.02 in the wrong direction, one-sided p = 0.62). An exploratory analysis restricted to post-win trials, where the effect is concentrated, found a small positive association with impulsivity (r(437) = 0.11, p = 0.023; Spearman ρ(437) = 0.13, p = 0.008), which does not survive controlling for the decline in switching over trials (each participant's ITI slope from the mixed-effects model with the linear trial term: r(437) = 0.08, p = 0.11).

To test whether our findings generalize to existing similar studies, we first showed that our main effect was replicable in an independent dataset without the ITI-bytrial confound. Specifically, in a new Study 4, we expected that the ITI effect would be stronger after a win than after a loss even when longer ITIs were no longer more common toward the start of the experiment. We ran the task of Study 3 unchanged except for the fixed sequence of ITIs, which was constructed against the hypothesis: 26 of the 50 ITIs in the first half of the task were short and 26 of the 50 in the second half long, with five or six short ITIs in every block of ten trials in the first half and the mirror image in the second (Fig. 5c). Long ITIs were therefore no longer concentrated where switching is highest. Participants learned as before (chose-best rate 0.45, t(116) = 13.7, p < 10⁻²⁵) and switching declined as before, from 63% over the first twenty trials to 41% over the last twenty (withinparticipant slope 0.26 per 100 trials, t(116) = 8.1, p < 10 --⁻¹²).

As predicted, switching after a win rose significantly, from 28.1% to 32.3% (t(116) = 3.74, p = 0.0003), and after a loss it was absent (72.6% to 71.5%, t(116) = 0.77, p = -0.45; the two effects differed, t(116) = 2.90, p = 0.004; Fig. 5a). The effect after wins was again present both early and late in the task (Fig. 5b). The response-time pattern replicated as well: after a win a long ITI slowed staying relative to switching (ITI × stay, +0.069, CI = [0.037, 0.100]), whereas after a loss the shift went the other way ( 0.061, CI = [ 0.100, 0.021]; three-way interaction +0.128, CI = [0.079, ---0.178]). As in Studies 1-3, the ITI after the choice two trials back did not predict switching when that option differed from the last one (odds ratio 0.93, CI = [0.83, 1.06]; Supplementary Fig. 2).

The computational modeling of Study 4 mirrored that of Study 3 (see Supplemental Material), wherein the ITI-competes-with-value model was again the best-fitting model. Simulated from its fitted parameters, the winning model was again the only model whose effect after wins grew with exploratory state (Fig 4f). To demonstrate that our key hypothesis generalizes to existing studies, and was not a produce of our task-design choices, we sought to determine whether the key prediction of our model would be replicated in a publicly shared fMRI dataset. We chose the two-armed bandit of Tomov et al. 25 , in which 31 participants played a new pair of arms every ten trials over two scanned sessions, because its ITIs cover a range of similar width to ours (about 2.5 s, from 4.8 to 7.3 s), though shifted toward the longer intervals typical of fMRI, and are sampled uniformly across that range, which lets us estimate a continuous slope relating ITI length to choice switching. In a Bayesian mixed-effects model with participant-level random intercepts, ITI slopes and linear trends over the ten trials of each pair of arms, a longer ITI before the choice increased switching (b = 0.130 log-odds per second, CI = [0.004, 0.255]; posterior probability of a positive slope 0.98; Fig. 6a). The effect of the ITI on switching thus held in an independent dataset.

Ultimately, to ensure our effects were not biased by online dissemination, we asked whether online artificial agents might have been responsible for our findings, a documented and growing concern in online samples 26, 27 . We reasoned that leading models would not show our key result, because the effect of ITIs on reinforcement learning is absent from the literature these models are trained on and so is unlikely to be part of their imitation of human behavior. To test the hypothesis that LLMs would not display our key behavior, we had large language models (Claude Opus 5, Sonnet 5 and Haiku 4.5) play the Study 4 task through the live web page as naive participants 28, 29 . Each agent was a fresh conversation that saw only what a participant sees: the text of every screen from the consent form to the questionnaires, the outcome of each choice ("You won $1" or "You lost $1") and a screenshot of the task screen on its first practice trial and its first task trial. It had no access to the page's code or to the reward probabilities, and every prompt it received was logged. The trial order, outcomes and ITI sequence were exactly those of Study 4, and the ITI was described in words.

We tried several AI agents with different prompts and information regarding what the ITI was each trial and whether time might matter or not in this task. In the time-blind condition, the agent was not told the ITI. By contrast, in the time-told condition, the ITI was named ("shown for 4 seconds"). We also varied our attempt to promote human mimicry in behavior, by saying, in the opening instructions either "Play like a human would", or "Play like a human that is sensitive to time costs." Fourteen agents were run (six instruction × condition cells of one to three agents; total cost about $7).

The agents learned the task at least as well as people (Fig. 6f), yet also overexploited relative to humans (Fig. 6e). The post-win ITI effect that all four human studies show was not reflected in the agents' behavior. After wins the difference between 4 s and 1 s lay between 0.03 and +0.01 regardless of how we prompted the agents to pay attention to time in the task (Fig. 6c). After losses the differences ranged from 0.09 to +0.07 with standard errors as large, on 10 to 26 trials per agent and bar (Fig. 6d). Thus, neither being told the duration nor being told to be sensitive to time costs changed this. The reasoning summaries returned by the models tallied wins and losses for each option and never mentioned the ITI: none of the 148 reasoning summaries returned over all screens (142 of them on task trials) mentioned the wait, including those of agents told its duration and asked to be sensitive to time costs (Fig. 6b). of a pair of arms (mean ± s.e.m.

) and the model's trend (red). b, One trial of the Study 4 task as a languagemodel agent had it, verbatim from its run record (Claude Sonnet 5, time-told, instructed "Play like a human that is sensitive to time costs"; trial 15, a win followed by a 4 s ITI). Left to right: the image of the screen, which each agent received only on its first practice and first task trial; the text message it received on every trial (in the time-blind condition, the same message without the duration of the fixation cross); the summary of its reasoning returned by the model's API; and its reply, which the harness entered as a key press on the live task page while the page's clock was stopped. Below the reasoning, the number of reasoning summaries, over all 14 agents, that mention the wait.

Discussion

Across four behavioral studies, we found that longer inter-trial intervals (ITIs) increased the likelihood of switching between options in a reinforcement-learning task, particularly following rewarding outcomes. This effect emerged even though waiting times were independent of participants' choices. Computational modeling favored an account in which the wait just experienced competes with reward values for control of the next choice. Our findings are consistent with the possibility that the influence of waiting time becomes stronger when reward values are more uncertain.

In foraging environments, the Marginal Value Theorem formalizes why waiting longer without reward in one's current environment increases the opportunity cost of foregoing switching to a potentially richer alternative. Switching between options in our task, however, could not reduce waiting time. That switching nevertheless increased with longer ITIs suggests that the influence of time on reinforcement learning may extend beyond situations in which waiting costs can be reduced through choice.

We had hypothesized that a longer ITI would give participants more time to replay a recent outcome, amplifying its recency-weighted influence and increasing the tendency to stay with a rewarded choice. Instead, switching after a win increased with longer ITIs -the opposite of this prediction. The replay account was further undermined by Study 2, in which filling the ITI with a demanding secondary task, thought to reduce offline replay, left the effect essentially unchanged.

These findings suggest that mechanisms other than replay may account for the effect of waiting time on choice. Longer waits might weaken the tendency to repeat previously chosen actions, independently of their outcomes, much as sensory representations decay over time 15 (the ITI-on-choice-bias model). This account is inconsistent with the evidence that the ITI effect was value-dependent, as it was concentrated after wins. Moreover, it persisted in a study that had a secondary task during the ITI, and which required creating new and competing action representations that likely would interfere with the RL choice representations. Alternatively, waiting time might have acted as a cost that reduces the value of the previously chosen option, regardless of whether it was rewarded. Learning to take actions by subtracting waiting time from earned reward is akin to the opportunity cost of time in average-reward reinforcement learning 30 . Neither of these accounts, however, readily explains why the ITI effect was stronger following rewarding outcomes.

Instead, computational modeling favored an account in which the ITI competes with value. After a longer ITI, part of the weight of the next decision shifts from learned reward values to the wait just experienced, which counts against the action that preceded it. The model further suggests that waiting time may carry greater weight when choices are less guided by learned reward values, potentially reflecting greater uncertainty about those values. A corresponding asymmetry in response times, which were not used to fit the model, provided additional support for this account.

To test the generalizability of these findings, we examined an independent fMRI dataset from Tomov et al. 25 , in which ITIs were varied for imaging purposes rather than to investigate their effects on learning. Consistent with our results, longer ITIs were associated with increased switching, with an effect in the same direction and of a similar order of magnitude to that observed in Study 3. These findings suggest that continuously varied ITIs, which are near-universal in fMRI designs, can affect learning and decision-making.

Large language-model agents given the same screens, outcomes, and instructions did not show the post-win ITI effect observed in human participants. In their trialby-trial reasoning, agents referred to the history of wins and losses for each option but did not mention ITI duration. These findings raise questions about the conditions under which artificial agents incorporate temporal information into their decisions, and how these processes compare with those observed in humans.

Several limitations qualify our main conclusions. In Studies 1-3, all participants received the same ITI sequence, with longer intervals occurring more frequently early in the task, when switching was also highest, confounding ITI duration with trial number. Study 4 reversed this ITI distribution and replicated the main effect, arguing against trial number as its sole driver. Although we found no evidence that earlier ITIs influenced switching away from other options, the fixed ITI sequence limits our ability to rule out a global waiting-time expectation; testing this account more conclusively will require ITIs randomized within participants. A gap of a different kind appears in the model itself: the ITI-competes-with-value model underestimated the post-win ITI effect for frequently chosen options and missed the small negative ITI slope after losses in Study 3, so its account of the effect is incomplete. This gap sits precisely where we judged reward values to be most certain, which points to a related limitation: reward uncertainty was inferred indirectly from choice history rather than measured or manipulated, so its contribution to the ITI effect remains to be tested directly. More broadly, our experimental manipulation contrasted only two fixed ITIs in online, Englishspeaking samples; the Tomov et al. 25 dataset extends the effect to a different range of intervals and an independent sample, but its generalizability to shorter intervals and other populations remains to be established.

Together, these findings suggest that the ITI influences reinforcement learning even when it is independent of one's choices. This may reflect the operation of a naturalistic prior to maximize reward per unit time, even when time to earn reward, or seek a new state in one's environment, is not under one's control.

Methods

Participants

Participants in all four studies were recruited through Prolific 31 . Eligibility was restricted to people who held nationality in an English-speaking country (United Kingdom, United States, Ireland, Australia, Canada or New Zealand). They also had to report English as a fluent language and have a Prolific approval rate of 95-100%. Each study excluded from its recruitment pool everyone who had taken part in an earlier study or pilot of the project, so no participant took part in more than one study. Participants received £1.20 for a session estimated at about 10 minutes. They were told that they would receive a performance-based bonus calculated from 10 randomly selected trials; in practice, every participant received the same flat bonus, irrespective of their outcomes. All studies were approved by the Human Subjects Institutional Review Board (HSIRB) of Bar-Ilan University (approval no. 310725687), and all participants gave informed consent online before starting the task.

In Study 1, the 96 analyzed participants were aged 24 to 81 years (M = 46.2, SD = 13.0); 54 were women and 42 men. For Studies 2 and 3, the figures below describe everyone who submitted the study on Prolific (99 and 481 people), not only the analyzed samples. In Study 2, ages ranged from 22 to 74 years (M = 45.7, SD = 13.6). There were 54 women and 44 men, and one participant preferred not to report their sex. In Study 3, ages ranged from 18 to 76 years (M = 40.0, SD = 13.0). There were 246 men and 231 women, and four participants preferred not to report their sex. In Study 4, the 117 analyzed participants reported ages of 19 to 82 years (M = 43.0, SD = 13.2) during the task.

No exclusion criterion was preregistered. Every analysis uses the participants whose session reached at least trial 90 of the 100, that is, who completed at least 90% of the task. This rule kept 96 of the 101 participants with trial data in Study 1, all 96 in Study 2, 439 of 488 in Study 3 and 117 of 135 in Study 4. Within an included session, a missed response (no choice within the 2 s deadline) removed that trial and the choice immediately after it from every analysis. No switch can be scored without a choice on the preceding trial. No included participant missed more than five trials. In Study 2, a choice faster than 250 ms was treated in the same way as a missed response. A downward dot-motion display was answered by pressing Q, T and P together, which are also the three choice keys. A press that came after the display had ended therefore landed on the next choice screen, where the first of the three keys to go down registered as a choice. Such choices were impossibly fast, did not follow the values the participant had learned and switched at the chance level of 2/3 (Fig. 2d-f). They were also several times more common than in Study 1: after a 1 s ITI, 11.3% of Study 2 choices came within 250 ms, compared to 2.5% in Study 1. The rule removed 6.7% of Study 2 choices and, with each, the switch scored on the next trial. It was applied to every Study 2 analysis and to no other study, because only Study 2 had a response inside the ITI. Analyses that condition on particular trial sequences, for example a valid choice on three consecutive trials, use the participants who contributed at least one such sequence, and the n of each analysis is reported with its result.

Task

All four studies used the same three-armed restless bandit task 6 , with 100 trials (Fig. 1a). On each trial three images were presented, and participants selected one by pressing Q (left), T (middle) or P (right) within a 2 s response deadline. Feedback was then displayed over the chosen image for 1,250 ms. It indicated a gain or a loss of $1 in virtual currency, which did not affect payment (Participants). Trials on which no response was registered within the deadline were recorded as misses, and participants were told in advance that the task would end if they accumulated five misses. The reward probability of each option drifted independently across trials as a Gaussian random walk. Its mean on each trial equaled the probability on the preceding trial, its standard deviation was 0.06, and it was reflected at bounds of 0.1 and 0.9 (Fig. 1b). All participants were exposed to the same predetermined trajectories, so the reward probabilities changed identically, and at the same points in the task, for everyone. The outcome of each choice was drawn independently for each participant from the current reward probability of the chosen option. Participants therefore shared the same probability environment but not the same sequence of wins and losses. Trials were separated by an intertrial interval (ITI) of either 1 s or 4 s, 50 of each, in a predetermined sequence. The sequence was identical for all participants and, in Studies 1-3, for all three studies. One property of this sequence matters for the analyses. Long ITIs were more frequent early in the session: 70%, 60%, 40%, 40% and 40% of the trials in successive blocks of twenty were followed by a 4 s ITI (Fig. 3c). Switching, in turn, declines over the session in every study. Before the main task, participants completed six practice trials with a different set of images and a different set of reward trajectories, and they were told that the images would change.

In Study 1, the ITI was an unfilled waiting period during which a central fixation cross was shown. By contrast, in Study 2, the ITI was filled by a perceptual task (Fig. 2a). After the outcome, a fixation cross was shown for 500 ms, followed by a random-dot-motion display 32 for the full duration of that trial's ITI (1 s or 4 s). The display consisted of 500 white dots (2 px) moving within a circular aperture scaled to the screen (the smaller of 60% of the viewport height, 60% of its width, or 600 px). It was refreshed at the screen frame rate of about 60 Hz. On each frame, each dot moved in the signal direction with probability 0.07 and in a random direction otherwise (7% coherence). Dots reaching the aperture boundary were repositioned at the opposite edge. Net motion was upward or downward in a fixed, predetermined sequence, identical for all participants, that placed 25 upward and 25 downward displays within the short-ITI trials and the same within the long-ITI trials. The response mapping was asymmetric. Downward motion required pressing Q, T and P simultaneously, and upward motion required withholding any response, so an ITI that elapsed without a simultaneous press was scored as an "up" response. No feedback on motion discrimination was given during the main task. Practice had three stages in a fixed order. Participants first completed six bandit trials with a fixation cross during the ITI. They then saw ten motion displays alone, at the same 1 s and 4 s durations, each followed by 1 s of accuracy feedback. Finally, they completed six trials of the combined task without motion feedback.

In Study 3, the ITI was unfilled, as in Study 1, and three things differed. First, the reward trajectories were generated under additional constraints. The trajectories started from probabilities of 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75. A set was accepted only if the highest-valued option changed exactly six times across the 100 trials, with consecutive changes at least 10 trials apart, and if each option was the highestvalued option at least once. The practice trajectories were a separate set starting from 0.75, 0.50 and 0.25. Second, misses during practice counted toward the fivemiss rule, whereas in Studies 1 and 2 the count was reset at the start of the main task. Third, participants reported their age before practice and their birth year after the task. A discrepancy of more than two years was recorded as a dataquality flag (five participants) but did not lead to exclusion. Study 3 was preregistered (https://osf.io/6tmja/overview). The preregistration specified the main effect of the ITI on switching, the individual-difference hypotheses and their directions, and no exclusion criterion.

In Study 4 the reward trajectories and procedure of Study 3 was unchanged except for the sequence of ITIs. This sequence was constructed against the hypothesis, so that long ITIs no longer coincided with the early part of the session, where switching is highest. In the first half of the task, 26 of the 50 ITIs were short, and in the second half 26 of the 50 were long. Every block of ten trials held five or six short ITIs in the first half and the mirror image in the second. No more than four identical ITIs occurred in a row, and no strictly alternating run was longer than seven. The share of 4 s ITIs in successive blocks of twenty trials was 45, 50, 50, 50 and 55%, against 70, 60, 40, 40 and 40% in Studies 1-3 (Fig. 5c). Study 4 was preregistered (https://osf.io/hvzsc/overview).

Questionnaires

In Studies 3 and 4, trait impulsivity was assessed after the task with an 8-item subset of the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11) 33 , using items 1, 2, 5, 8, 9, 12, 14 and 19. Items were rated on the standard 4-point scale from 1 ("rarely/never") to 4 ("almost always/always"). Items 1, 8, 9 and 12 were reverse-scored, and scores were summed (range 8-32, higher scores indicating greater impulsivity). An attention-check item instructing participants to select the third response option was embedded after the fourth item and scored separately. One participant in each study failed it and was flagged but not excluded. Anhedonia was assessed with the 14 items of the Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale (SHAPS) 34 , rated on a 4point agree-disagree scale. Each item scored 1 for any degree of disagreement and 0 for any degree of agreement, and items were summed (range 0-14, higher scores indicating greater anhedonia). Studies 1 and 2 instead collected the abbreviated Penn State Worry Questionnaire and the Anxious Arousal subscale of the Mood and Anxiety Symptom Questionnaire, which are not analyzed here.

Behavioral analyses

Switching. A switch was scored on every trial t > 1 on which a valid choice was registered on both t and t 1 and the option chosen differed from the option chosen on t 1. Because a missed trial breaks the sequence, the ITI preceding a choice is always exactly the interval that separated it from the previous choice. Effects of the ITI are indexed to this preceding interval, which we call the prior ITI.

Learning.

Learning was indexed by the probability of choosing the option with the highest current reward probability (the chose-best rate according to objective relative frequencies of winning and losing). This rate was compared with chance (1/3) by a one-sample t test across participants and shown over the session as a 5trial moving average (Fig. 1c).

Switching.

In Study 4, the decline of switching over the session was summarized by each participant's least-squares slope of switching on trial number, expressed per 100 trials and tested against zero across participants.

Accuracy in Study 2's perceptual decision-making task.

In Study 2, accuracy on the motion-discrimination task was computed per participant for the 1 s and the 4 s displays and compared by a paired t test.

Simple ITI analyses.

For each participant, the probability of switching was computed after short (1 s) and after long (4 s) prior ITIs, and the two were compared by a paired t test. The same contrast was computed separately on trials that followed a win and on trials that followed a loss. The difference between the post-win and post-loss effects was tested within participants by a paired t test. We also checked that the effect was robust to influences bound to time on task, such as the shift from early to late learning and fatigue. To do so, the paired tests after wins and after losses were repeated in the first and in the second half of the session (trials 2-50 and 51-100) in every study. In Study 3 this also tests the effect where the ITI sequence is nearly unrelated to trial number. From trial 41 on, the sequence held 40% long ITIs in every block of twenty trials, and the correlation between a long ITI and trial number was 0.05 in trials 51-100, against 0.15 in -trials 1-50. All t tests are two-sided unless stated otherwise.

Linear mixed-model of ITI effect.

Because the fixed ITI sequence of Studies 1-3 was front-loaded with long ITIs while switching declined over the session, every mixed-effects model includes a linear effect of trial number. The preregistered mixed-effects logistic regression of switching on the prior ITI was extended accordingly: logit P(switch_ij) = (β0 + u0,j) + (βITI + uITI,j) • ITI_ij + (βT + uT,j) • trial_ij, where ITI_ij is the prior ITI of participant j's choice i in seconds and trial_ij is the trial number centered and scaled per 50 trials ((t 50.5)/50). Each enters as a fixed effect and as a participant-level random slope. Other contrasts, for example the ITI after the choice two trials back (below), enter in the same way, with the trial term in every model. Every mixed-effects regression was fitted as a Bayesian model in PyMC 35 with the No-U-Turn sampler 36 (nutpie 37 ), using four chains of 1,000 draws after 1,000 warm-up iterations and a target acceptance of 0.9. Priors were N(0, 1.5) on the intercept, N(0, 1) on the other fixed effects and half-normal(1) on the random-effect standard deviations. Random effects were independent and in a non-centered parameterization. The random ITI slope varies little between participants, so its correlations with the other random effects are not identified.

For each effect we report the posterior mean and the 95% credible interval, written CI = [lower, upper], on the log-odds scale or as an odds ratio for 4 s against 1 s.

Every model reported has R m 1.1 for its fixed effects and random-effect standard ≤ deviations. The effect of the ITI after wins and after losses was estimated in those trials separately, and the difference between them by the prior ITI × previous outcome interaction in all trials. Each participant's ITI slope from this model, the posterior mean of the fixed plus random effect, is the participant-level effect used in the individual-difference analyses below.

Ruling out a global ITI effect.

A global expectation of waits predicts that an ITI should affect decisions about options other than the one it followed. We tested this on every trial on which the option chosen k trials back (k = 2, 3 or 4) differed from the option chosen last, with the k preceding trials responded and consecutive. On these trials, switching was related to the ITI that had followed that earlier choice (4 s against 1 s), whatever the last ITI. The mixed-effects model was switch ~ ITI k back + last ITI + trial + (1 + ITI k back + trial | participant), with the last ITI centered (Supplementary Fig. 1). Like the main effect, this contrast inherits the decline in switching through the front-loaded sequence, which the trial term absorbs. In Study 3, trials whose earlier ITI was long came on average from trial 41, and those whose earlier ITI was short from trial 54. The mean trial number of each trial type is reported descriptively.

ITI effect as a function of choice uncertainty.

As a model-agnostic proxy for whether a choice was exploratory or exploitative, we used how recently the chosen option had been chosen. For the option chosen on trial t, u_t = 1/(1 + n_t), where n_t counts the option's earlier choices. The count rises by one each time the option is chosen and loses a fraction λ = 0.85 of its size on every trial on which the option is not chosen. The post-win trend reported held for every λ between 0.5 and 0.9 in both studies (all p 0.003); the weak post-loss trend in Study 3 did not (p = 0.23 at ≤ λ = 0.5). The ITI-competes-with-value model (below) uses the limiting case λ = 1, in which n_t is the number of consecutive choices of the option. u is near 1 when the option had not been chosen on the last trial or two, and it approaches 0 when the option had been chosen repeatedly. The proxy is consistent with the explore and exploit states of a hidden Markov model of choices alone 38 . The within-participant rank correlation between u and the filtered probability of the explore state was 0.93 on post-win and 0.87 on post-loss trials in both studies. Post-win and post-loss trials were divided into quintiles of u within each participant, with ties in random order. The effect of the ITI on switching, the probability after 4 s minus after 1 s, was then computed per quintile and participant. Its dependence on u was tested by each participant's least-squares slope over the quintiles (one-sample t test). The same measure was computed on data simulated from every computational model (Model fitting and comparison).

Determining whether RT behavior is consistent with ITI effect on choice.

Response times were not used in fitting any model. The ITI-on-choice-bias model and the ITI-as-learning-target model predict that a long wait slows staying relative to switching after wins and after losses alike, whereas the ITI-competes-with-value model predicts this shift after wins only (Computational models). We tested this with a Bayesian linear mixed model of log response time, fitted as above with a Gaussian likelihood, on scored trials with response times of at least 150 ms. The predictors were the prior ITI (centered), the previous outcome, whether the current choice was a stay, all their interactions, and trial number. The model had participant random intercepts and random slopes on trial number, and it was then fitted separately after wins and after losses. Responses are also faster overall after a long ITI. This speed-up is expected from temporal preparation (the variableforeperiod effect) 39 and is not predicted by any of the models, so it is not used as evidence.

Individual differences in psychopathology.

Study 3 preregistered a positive association between impulsivity and the ITI effect and a negative association between anhedonia and the ITI effect. Each was tested by a one-sided Pearson correlation with the participant-level ITI effect, the difference in switching after 4 s and after 1 s over all trials. We report as exploratory the association of impulsivity with the post-win effect, by Pearson and Spearman correlation, and with each participant's ITI slope from the mixed-effects model with the linear trial term. Associations between the two questionnaire scores and the participant-level posterior means of the winning computational model's parameters were assessed by Spearman correlations in Studies 3 and 4, with Benjamini-Hochberg falsediscovery-rate correction 40 over the full set of tests.

Computational models

The behavioral results show that a long ITI after a choice makes participants more likely to leave that option, and that this holds after wins and not after losses. The models ask where the ITI acts. On a first account, the ITI enters the value of the option that preceded it. The wait is then a cost, and an option whose outcome was followed by a long wait is learned to be worth less. On a second account, the ITI leaves value untouched and weakens the tendency to repeat the last action, as a fading trace of that action would. Both predict more switching after long ITIs, but they differ in what else should change. A third possibility is a single learned expectation of how long waits are in the task as a whole. We tested it modelagnostically through the carry-over contrast above and did not model it. Because the ITI sequence was identical for all participants, such a global expectation is largely confounded with position in the session in this design, and testing it requires ITIs randomized within participants. The third model we fitted, the ITIcompetes-with-value model, was instead built on the finding that the ITI acts most on exploratory choices. Each model is named by what it adds to the model it builds on, and Supplementary Table 1 lists every model with its parameters.

All models share the same structure. On trial t the participant chooses one of three options, a_t, and receives an outcome r t , coded +1 for a win and 1 for a loss.

- where v t (a) collects the terms described below.

The ITI that followed trial t is coded w t = 0 after a 1 s ITI and 1 after a 4 s ITI, so only the long wait enters the models. A wait can thus be a cost but never a benefit, and the short ITI is the reference against which the long one is measured. Values start at 0, the neutral value midway between a win and a loss, and decay toward it. Coding the outcomes 1 and 0 instead would therefore change only the scale of the inverse temperature and of the time cost (the fixed cost of the wait would become 0.5, half the outcome unit), not any prediction of any model. As in the behavioral analyses, a missed trial is skipped. The choice made right after it does not enter the likelihood and receives no bias toward the previous choice, but its outcome still updates learning. The session trend covariate is τ t = ( tria l t -50.5 ) / 50 , with trial_t the trial number.

The models were built in stages on Study 3, the preregistered study with the largest sample. Here we write equations for each addition to the model comparison. Each stage added one component and kept it only if it improved outof-sample predictive accuracy by more than two standard errors of the paired difference (Model fitting and comparison). The first stage asked how participants learn the values of the options. The baseline has no learning, only fixed preferences for the three options ( v t (a)=c a , with c3 = 0 ). The simplest learner, a Rescorla-Wagner model 41 , updates the value of the chosen option by its prediction error, Q t +1 =Q t ( a t ) + α• ( r t -Q t ( a t )), where, when included in the softmax choice function, was multiplied by an inverse temperature β• Q t (a) to control exploration and exploitation.

The next model allowed separate learning rates after a win (α ⁺) and after a loss ( α ⁺). Finally, because the reward probabilities drift, the values of unchosen options decay back toward the neutral value by a factor d on every trial, Q t +1 = d• Q t (a) for a ≠ a t (value decay). Each addition was kept.

People also tend to repeat what they have chosen, and we compared two ways of capturing this, each added to the value learner. A constant stay bias adds a fixed amount s to the decision value of the option chosen last. A choice kernel keeps a running trace of how often each option has been chosen recently, a) ), where x t (a) = 1if a was chosen and 0 otherwise and traces start at 0.5. It adds β C • C t (a) to every option's decision value 24 . These terms are alternatives, and the one with the better predictive accuracy, the choice kernel, was carried forward.

Posterior predictive checks of the choice-bias models showed that after switching away from an option, participants moved on to the third option, the one they had not just left, more often than any model predicted. We therefore added a bonus for the option chosen furthest back. On every trial, the option whose last choice lies furthest in the past receives a constant bonus , v t (a) + = ω . An option never chosen counts as chosen before the first trial, and if two options tie, both receive the bonus. The bonus acts on choice, not on learned value, and pulls the opposite way from the choice kernel.

Switching falls over the session in every study, and we compared two ways of letting behavior change with time on task. The exploration trend lets the inverse temperature change log-linearly with trial number , β t = β•exp ( κ β • τ t ), so that choices become more ( κ β > 0 ) or less driven by value as the session goes on. The choice-bias trend applies the same form to the weight of the choice kernel, β C • exp ( κ b • τ t ). The exploration trend predicted better and was carried forward. A novelty bonus captured the pull toward options that had not been tried recently.

The option chosen furthest back, or one not yet chosen, received a constant bonus ωadded to its decision value, ω• 1 [ a = mi n k L t ( k ) ], where L t ( k ) is the trial on which option k was last chosen. When options tied for furthest back, each received the bonus. With ω > 0, choices are drawn toward the least recently sampled option, independently of its learned value, since the bonus is not scaled by the inverse temperature. The novelty bonus predicted better than the model without it in both studies and was carried forward. The last stage added the ITI in three forms, each of which reduces exactly to the model without an ITI term when its ITI parameter is zero. In the ITI-as-learningtarget model, an additive time cost, the long wait that followed an outcome is subtracted from the value learned from it. The chosen option is updated toward y t =r t -c• w t instead of r t , so with c > 0 any outcome followed by a long wait is learned as worth less, by the same amount after a win and after a loss.

In the ITI-on-choice-bias model, the ITI leaves values untouched and scales the strength of the choice bias on the next choice, v t (a) + = β C • exp ( γ• w t -1 ) • C t (a) . With γ < 0 the pull toward the options chosen most often is weaker after a long ITI, whatever the outcome was.

In the ITI-competes-with-value model, the wait just experienced is itself evidence on the next choice and counts as a cost of 1 against the option chosen before it. After a long ITI, a share π_t of the inverse temperature moves from the values to this wait on the next choice,

And where the weight on the ITI effect was modulated by uncertainty ( u t -1 ) on the last trial where the last iti ( w t -1 ) was experienced: π t = κ• u t -1 • w t -1 , Above, 1 [ a = a t -1 ]is 1 for the option chosen before the ITI and 0 for the others. The term u t -1 = 1 / ( 1 + n t -1 ( a t -1 )) refers to the option before its most-recent choice, with n t (a) the number of consecutive choices of a just before trial t. This is the count of the exploratory-state proxy with λ = 1, sou = 1 after a switch to the option, 1/2 after two choices of it in a row, and so on. After a 1 s ITI nothing moves. After a 4 s ITI the shift is largest when the option just chosen had just been switched to, that is, after an exploratory choice. The cost of the wait time is estimated as a free parameter, κ. The final comparison included the model without an ITI term and the three ITI models.

Model fitting and comparison

Every model was fitted to Study 3 and, separately, to Study 4 as a hierarchical Bayesian model in PyMC 35 with the No-U-Turn sampler 36 (nutpie 37 ). The fits used the main samples, each participant with their own ITI sequence, reward trajectories and missed trials. Priors were non-centered and independent per parameter, with z i ~ N (0,1) for participant i and σ ~ halfNormal (1). Parameters on the unit interval (learning rates, decay and κ) had the priors θ i = logit ⁺ ¹ ( μ + σ z i ) with μ ~N (0,1.5). Positive parameters (the inverse temperature and the choice-kernel weight) had the priors θ i = exp ( μ + σ z i ) with μ ~N (0.5,1). Real-valued parameters (intercepts, the stay bias, trends, the time cost, γ and the novelty bonus) had the priors θ i = μ + σ z i with μ ~N (0,1).

Four chains of 1,000 draws followed 2,000 warm-up iterations, with a target acceptance of 0.9. In Study 4, the model without an ITI term and the ITI-competeswith-value model were refitted with four chains of 2,000 draws after 4,000 warmup iterations, because the spread of the choice-kernel learning rate mixed slowly. Every group-level parameter in the winning model had R m 1.07, including the ITI ≤ parameter of each model ( 1.05). Because the stage decisions were taken on ≤ Study 3 and held fixed, the Study 4 comparison is reported as a replication of their direction, with these values listed in Supplementary Table 1. In Study 3, a model could be carried forward or win a comparison only if the split-R m of every grouplevel parameter was at most 1.1, and divergent transitions were counted for every fit. Participant-level parameters are summarized by their posterior means. Grouplevel values are summarized by the posterior mean and 95% credible interval of the group location μ, transformed to the parameter's scale. The likelihood is written once and shared by the sampler, the simulators and an independent reference implementation, against which it is tested for every model. Every model reduces exactly to the model it extends when its added parameters take their null values.

Models were compared by Pareto-smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO) 42 on the trial-level log-likelihoods. Each participant's first trial was excluded, because its probability is 1/3 under every learning model. We report the expected log predictive density (ELPD) and, for every pair of models compared, the difference in ELPD with the standard error of the paired pointwise difference. Within the value-learning stage, each addition was compared with the model it extends. Between the two choice-bias terms, and between the two trends, the one with the larger ELPD was taken. A component was carried forward only if it improved on its parent by more than two standard errors. The stage decisions were taken on Study 3 and held fixed for Study 4. Every model was also compared with the best model of the sequence (Fig. 4a; Supplementary Table 1). The final comparison between the model without an ITI term and the three ITI models was complemented, as a sensitivity analysis, by random-effects Bayesian model selection on the participant-level summed ELPD 43, 44 . For this comparison we report the protected exceedance probability (PXP), the Bayesian omnibus risk and the number of participants best fitted by each model.

Every modelling addition was simulated to generate the intended model-agnostic effect (Fig. 4b). Each participant was simulated 20 times from their posterior-mean parameters in their own task environment, that is, with their reward trajectories, the ITI sequence and their missed trials. The same behavioral measures were then computed on the simulated and the real data. Value learning was checked against the share of choices given to the currently best option in 10-trial windows, using the root-mean-square error between simulated and observed curves. The choicebias terms were checked against switching after a stay and after a switch on the previous trial. They were also checked against the share of switches after a switch that returned to the option chosen two trials earlier. The trend was checked against the probability of switching in 10-trial windows. The ITI models were checked in each study separately, first against the ITI slope of the mixed-effects model with the linear trial term (Fig. 4c). This model was fitted in the same way to the real data and to each of the 20 simulated datasets, with two chains of 500 draws per simulated dataset. The slopes after wins and after losses came from the model with the prior ITI × previous outcome interaction. The ITI models were also checked against the exploratory-state proxy, that is, the post-win and post-loss ITI effect by quintile of u and its per-participant trend across quintiles (Fig. 4f). A model is judged by whether the observed value falls within the 95% range of its 20 simulated datasets. The model without an ITI term, simulated in the same way, shows how much of the raw ITI effect the front-loaded sequence of Study 3 produces on its own.

Parameter and model recovery were run on Study 3 with the priors and settings of the real fits (Fig. 4d,e). For parameter recovery of the ITI-competes-with-value model, each participant's task environment was played once by a synthetic participant. Every parameter of that synthetic participant was drawn independently and uniformly over its full range, and the synthetic participants were refitted with the same hierarchy. Recovery is the correlation between generating and recovered participant posterior means. For model recovery among the three ITI models, five datasets of 50 synthetic participants were simulated from each model. Each synthetic participant played a randomly chosen real participant's task, with parameters spread evenly over the full range of every parameter (Latinhypercube sampling 45 ). All three models were fitted to every dataset, and a dataset was scored as recovered when the generating model had the highest summed ELPD.

External dataset

To test the effect in an independent dataset, we searched public repositories (OpenNeuro 46 , OSF, GitHub and figshare) for trial-level data from reinforcementlearning tasks in which the interval preceding each choice varied. Three criteria were fixed before any analysis. First, the task had to involve learning under changing reward contingencies, so that participants tracked option values rather than reading them off the screen. Second, the interval had to vary on the scale of seconds, so that effects could be compared per second of interval with our 1 s versus 4 s manipulation. Third, we looked for fMRI designs, because jittered intertrial intervals are near-universal in neuroimaging, where they are introduced to decorrelate regressors 8 and are not entered into the behavioral model. Most candidates were ruled out because the interval was fixed, timing was not recorded or the chosen option could not be recovered from the event files. Among the datasets that met the criteria, we analyzed the one in which the interval was sampled uniformly across a range of similar width to our manipulation, Tomov et al. 25 . In the others, the interval varied over only about one second or took almost only two values, which leaves the slope per second resting on a single contrast.

The dataset of Tomov et al. 25 comes from the authors' repository (github.com/tomov/Exploration-Data-Analysis). Thirty-one participants completed two scanned sessions of a two-armed bandit in which each ten-trial run presented a new pair of arms with fixed but unknown means, under four risk conditions. Arm positions varied across runs, so option identity was taken from arm color. The blank interval after feedback was scheduled uniformly at random between 4.8 and 7.3 s. The realized interval was additionally adjusted online to keep the run on schedule and therefore depended on the participant's own response time, so the scheduled value was used as the predictor. A trial entered the analysis if a valid choice was registered on it and on the immediately preceding trial of the same ten-trial run. Because the first trial of a run has no preceding interval, it was dropped before the preceding trial was identified, so the scored trials of each run are trials 3-10. Switching was scored as choosing a different arm from the previous trial. As in our own studies, no participant was excluded.

Switching was modeled with the mixed-effects logistic regression of our own studies, fitted in the same way with the same priors and sampler: logitP ( switc h i p ) =( β 0 + u 0 , p)+( βITI + uITI , p) •I i p + ( βT + uT , p) • tria l i p , where ITI_ip is the scheduled interval before the choice in seconds, centered on participant p's median so that βITI reflects within-participant variation.

The term trial_ip is the trial within the current pair of arms, centered on the midpoint of the ten trials and scaled per ten trials ((trial 5.5)/10). The linear trend therefore describes the decline in switching across each pair of arms and starts afresh with every new pair. The terms u are participant-level random intercepts, ITI slopes and trends. Because the interval lies close to zero, this model was fitted with four chains of 10,000 draws after 2,000 warm-up iterations, which gave the same estimate to the third decimal in two independent runs. We report the posterior mean of βITI, its 95% credible interval and the posterior probability that βITI > 0. In Fig. 6a the observed switching rate is shown by quintile of the interval (mean ± s.e.m. across participants). The model's population-average curve was obtained by setting the interval to each value in turn and averaging the predicted probability over every participant's posterior-mean coefficients and every trial's position within its pair of arms. The trend curve was obtained in the same way, with the interval at each trial's observed value.

Language-model agents

We asked whether a learner that receives the same feedback but does not experience time shows the ITI effect. To this end, large language models (Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Haiku 4.5) 47 played the Study 4 task through the live web page as naive participants. A harness drove the page with a browserautomation library (Playwright 48 ), with one fresh API conversation per agent. Replies were constrained by structured output to the answer each screen required, whether a key press, a questionnaire response or a free-text field. Each agent saw only what a participant sees: the text of every screen from the consent form to the questionnaires, the outcome of each choice ("You won $1" or "You lost $1") and a screenshot of the task screen on its first practice trial and its first task trial. It had no access to the page's code or to the reward probabilities, and every prompt and reply was logged. Because a model cannot answer within the 2 s deadline, the page's clock was frozen while the agent chose and then advanced through the feedback and the ITI. The trial order, outcomes and ITI sequence were therefore exactly those of Study 4, but the recorded response times are meaningless and were not analyzed. The ITI was described in words. In the time-blind condition the description omitted its duration, so any ITI effect could only come from the structure of the task. In the time-told condition it named the duration ("shown for 4 seconds"). One sentence added to the opening instructions varied between runs: none, "Play like a human would.", or "Play like a human that is sensitive to time costs." Fourteen agents were run (Opus 5 × 6, Sonnet 5 × 4, Haiku 4.5 × 4), in six instruction × condition cells of one to three agents. Their records were saved in the format of Study 4 and scored with the same scripts. The measures were the chosebest rate, switching after a win and after a loss following each ITI, and switching over the session in 10-trial bins. With 14 agents, these measures are reported descriptively, as means and standard errors across agents and as single-agent values, alongside the human values of Study 4. The two agents of the cell without an added sentence (Claude Opus 5, one per condition) were pilot runs made before a fix to the harness, and some of their replies contained text beyond the key press (in one of them, an invented description of the next screen). Their key presses were nevertheless read correctly; they are included among the 14 agents and marked as pilot runs in the shared data. The cell "Play like a human would." pairs different models in its two conditions (time-blind: Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 × 2; time-told: Opus 5 and Haiku 4.5 × 2), so it is not a clean comparison of the conditions.

Statistics and software

Paired and one-sample t tests are two-sided unless stated otherwise, and correlations are Pearson's r unless stated otherwise. For frequentist tests we report the test statistic with its degrees of freedom and the p value. For every Bayesian model we report the posterior mean and the 95% credible interval, written CI = [lower, upper]. Convergence is judged by the split-R m of the fixed effects and random-effect standard deviations in mixed-effects models, and of the grouplevel parameters in computational models, with a threshold of 1.1. The number of divergent transitions is recorded for every fit. Behavioral analyses were run in Python, with SciPy 49 for t tests and correlations and statsmodels 50 for falsediscovery-rate correction. Every mixed-effects logistic and linear regression and every computational model was fitted in PyMC 35 with the nutpie sampler 37 , and PSIS-LOO was computed in ArviZ 51 .

The likelihoods, simulators and random-effects Bayesian model selection are implemented in Python (Python 3.13.13, PyMC 6.3.1, nutpie 0.16.11, ArviZ 1.3.0, SciPy 1.18.0, statsmodels 0.15.0). The task code, data, analysis code and every reported number are available at https://github.com/sharplabBIU/iti_learning.
